sentences.text: Austriadraco dallavecchiai is an extinct genus of pterosaur known from a small species with a humerus length of about four centimetres, while the shinbone measures 57.7 millimetres.

The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — consists of a partial and disarticulated skeleton that includes a skull with frontal bones, lower jaws, loose teeth, vertebrae from the neck to the tail, the shoulder girdle, humeri, a wing phalanx, the pelvis, and leg bones.
The shoulder blade is 62% longer than the coracoid, and the shinbone reaches 70% of the humerus length and 92% of the first wing finger phalanx length.
Early analysis incorrectly identified the fused frontal bones as a breast bone.
Bernd Lammerer discovered the Austriadraco skeleton in June 1994 on a mountain trail near Seefeld in Austrian Tirol at an altitude of 1600 metres.
The fossil remains were recovered as five stone plates that were removed multiple times from the Seefeld Formation dating from the late Norian.
The fossil is now housed in the collection of the Bavarian State Collection for Palaeontology and Historical Geology in Munich.
Alexander Kellner named the genus Austriadraco in 2015, designating Austriadraco dallavecchiai as the type species.
The generic name Austriadraco combines the Latin words for Austria and dragon, while the specific name dallavecchiai honors Fabio Marco Dalla Vecchia.

Kellner placed Austriadraco in an undefined family called Austriadraconidae due to uncertain affinities, suggesting a close relationship with Arcticodactylus based on the shared trait of a short coracoid.
A 2020 study by Matthew G. Baron grouped Austriadraco with Carniadactylus and Raeticodactylus within the clade Caviramidae.
Austriadraco lived during the Late Triassic, specifically the Norian stage between 217 and 213 million years ago, in present-day Austria.

In 2003, Peter Wellnhofer initially identified the fossil as a specimen of Eudimorphodon ranzii, considering it a juvenile because it was 10 to 25% shorter than the holotype of that species. It is debated whether the specimen represents a juvenile of Eudimorphodon or a distinct genus, with Dalla Vecchia concluding it was neither in 2009.
